arXiv:2604.05403v1 [math.NT] 07 Apr 2026

Proof of a conjecture of Banerjee, Bringmann and Bachraoui on infinite families of congruences

Juejie Sun1 and Olivia X.M. Yao2

1,2School of Mathematical Sciences,

Suzhou University of Science and Technology,

Suzhou, 215009, Jiangsu Province, P. R. China

Email: jeric_\_020918@163.com, yaoxiangmei@163.com

Abstract. Recently, Andrews and Bachraoui investigated congruences for certain restricted two-color partitions. They made two conjectures for Ramanujan type congruences and a vanishing identity for the limiting sequence. Very recently, Banerjee, Bringmann and Bachraoui confirmed these three conjectures by relating the corresponding generating function to modular forms and mock theta functions. At the end of their paper, they posed a conjecture on infinite families of congruences modulo 4 and 8 for the limiting sequence. The Banerjee-Bringmann-Bachraoui’s conjecture implies the two conjectures given by Andrews and Bachraoui. In this note, we settle Banerjee-Bringmann-Bachraoui’s conjecture on infinite famlies of congruences based on Banerjee-Bringmann-Bachraoui’s results and an identity due to Waston.

Keywords: partitions, nonnegativity, qq-series.

AMS Subject Classification: 11P81, 05A17.

1 Introduction

A partition of a postive integer nn is a weakly decreasing sequence of positive integers π=(π1,π2,…,πk)\pi=(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\ldots,\pi_{k}) such that π1+π2+⋯+πk=n\pi_{1}+\pi_{2}+\cdots+\pi_{k}=n. The πi\pi_{i} are called the parts of partition. Let l⁡(π)l(\pi) and #⁡(π)\#(\pi) denote the largest part of π\pi and the number of parts of π\pi [1].

In recent years, integer partitions in which each part may occur in two colors have been studied ectensively, see for example [2, 3, 5, 4, 8]. In particular, Andrews and Bachraoui [3] invesigated sequences of integer partitions in two colors (blue and red), as in the following definition.

Definition 1.1.

Let kk be a fixed positive integer. For a positive integer nn, let c⁡(k,n)c(k,n) counts the number of two-color partitons π\pi of nn in which

  1. 1.

    the smallest part s⁡(π)s(\pi) is odd and occurs at least one in blue,

  2. 2.

    every even blue part is at least 2​k−12k-1 greater than s⁡(π)s(\pi),

  3. 3.

    the even parts of the same color are distinct.

Andrews and Bachraoui [3] established the generating function of c⁡(k,n)c(k,n)

Ck​(q):=∑n=0∞c⁡(k,n)​qn=∑n=0∞(−q2​n+2​k,−q2​n+2,q2)∞(q2​n+1,q2)∞2​q2​n+1.\displaystyle C_{k}(q):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c(k,n)q^{n}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-q^{2n+2k},-q^{2n+2};q^{2})_{\infty}}{(q^{2n+1};q^{2})_{\infty}^{2}}q^{2n+1}.

Here and throughout, we adopt the following standard qq-series notation:

(a,q)∞:=\displaystyle(a;q)_{\infty}:= ∏k=0∞(1−a​qk),(a,q)n:=(a,q)∞(a​qn,q)∞\displaystyle\prod_{k=0}^{\infty}(1-aq^{k}),\qquad(a;q)_{n}:=\frac{(a;q)_{\infty}}{(aq^{n};q)_{\infty}}

and

(a1,a2,…,ar;q)∞:=(a1;q)∞(a2;q)∞⋯(ar;q)∞.(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{r};q)_{\infty}:=(a_{1};q)_{\infty}(a_{2};q)_{\infty}\cdots(a_{r};q)_{\infty}.

Andrews and Bachraoui [3] proved a number of congruences modulo 4 on c⁡(k,n)c(k,n) for k=1,2,3k=1,2,3. At the end of their paper, they considered the congruence of the limits of Ck​(q)C_{k}(q). Let

C⁡(q):=limk→∞Ck​(q)=∑n=0∞(−q2​n+2,q2)∞(q2​n+1,q2)∞2​q2​n+1=:∑n=0∞c⁡(n)​qn.\displaystyle C(q):=\lim_{k\to\infty}C_{k}(q)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-q^{2n+2};q^{2})_{\infty}}{(q^{2n+1};q^{2})_{\infty}^{2}}q^{2n+1}=:\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c(n)q^{n}.

Andrews and Bachraoui [3] posed the following two conjectures.

Conjecture 1.2.

For n≥0n\geq 0,

c⁡(8​n+4)≡0(mod4).\displaystyle c(8n+4)\equiv 0\pmod{4}. (1.1)
Conjecture 1.3.

For n≥0n\geq 0,

c⁡(8​n+6)≡0(mod8).\displaystyle c(8n+6)\equiv 0\pmod{8}. (1.2)

Very recently, Banerjee, Bringmann and Bachraoui [4] proved Conjectures 1.2 and 1.3 by relating the corresponding generating function to modular forms and mock theta functions. They also showed that for n≥0n\geq 0,

c⁡(16​n+13)≡0(mod4).\displaystyle c(16n+13)\equiv 0\pmod{4}. (1.3)

At the end of their paper [4], Banerjee, Bringmann and Bachraoui presented the following two conjectures.

Conjecture 1.4.

For n≥0n\geq 0,

c⁡(32​n+23)≡0(mod8).\displaystyle c(32n+23)\equiv 0\pmod{8}. (1.4)
Conjecture 1.5.

For all integers nn and kk,

c⁡(22​k+3​n+11⋅4k+13)\displaystyle c\left(2^{2k+3}n+\frac{11\cdot 4^{k}+1}{3}\right) ≡0(mod4),\displaystyle\equiv 0\pmod{4}, (1.5)
c⁡(22​k+3​n+17⋅4k+13)\displaystyle c\left(2^{2k+3}n+\frac{17\cdot 4^{k}+1}{3}\right) ≡0(mod8),\displaystyle\equiv 0\pmod{8}, (1.6)
c⁡(22​k+4​n+38⋅4k+13)\displaystyle c\left(2^{2k+4}n+\frac{38\cdot 4^{k}+1}{3}\right) ≡0(mod4).\displaystyle\equiv 0\pmod{4}. (1.7)

Setting k=0k=0 in (1.5)–(1.7), we arrive at (1.1)–(1.3), respectively. Taking k=1k=1 in (1.6), we get (1.4). Therefore, Conjecture 1.5 implies Conjectures 1.2–1.4.

The aim of this paper is to confirm Conjecture 1.5 by utilizing Banerjee-Bringmann-Bachraoui’s results [4] and an identity due to Waston [12].

2 Proof of Conjecture 1.5

To prove Conjecture 1.5, we first prove two lemmas.

Lemma 2.1.

For all nonnegative integers nn and kk,

c⁡(22​k+2​n+22​k+3+13)≡(−1)k​c​(4​n+3)(mod8).\displaystyle c\left(2^{2k+2}n+\frac{2^{2k+3}+1}{3}\right)\equiv(-1)^{k}c(4n+3)\pmod{8}. (2.1)

Proof. In [4], Banerjee, Bringmann and Bachraoui proved that

C⁡(q)=2​q​f2​f4f12​B​(−q)−q​ω​(−q).\displaystyle C(q)=2q\frac{f_{2}f_{4}}{f_{1}^{2}}B(-q)-q\omega(-q). (2.2)

Here and throughout, for any psotive integer kk,

fm:=(qk,qk)∞.f_{m}:=(q^{k};q^{k})_{\infty}.

The third order mock theta function ω⁡(q)\omega(q) is defined by

ω⁡(q):=∑n=0∞q2​n​(n+1)(q,q2)n+12\omega(q):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{q^{2n(n+1)}}{(q;q^{2})_{n+1}^{2}}

and McIntosh’s second order mock theta function B⁡(q)B(q) [10] is defined by

B⁡(q):=∑n=0∞aB​(n)​qn=(−q2,q2)∞(q2,q2)∞​∑n=−∞∞(−1)n​q2​n​(n+1)1−q2​n+1=∑n=0∞(−q2,q2)n(q,q2)n+12​qn⁡(n+1).\displaystyle B(q):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{B}(n)q^{n}=\frac{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{\infty}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{\infty}}\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}q^{2n(n+1)}}{1-q^{2n+1}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}}{(q;q^{2})_{n+1}^{2}}q^{n(n+1)}. (2.3)

In [12], Watson proved that

f⁡(q8)−2​q​ω​(−q)−2​q3​ω​(−q4)=f12​f48f25​f84.\displaystyle f(q^{8})-2q\omega(-q)-2q^{3}\omega(-q^{4})=\frac{f_{1}^{2}f_{4}^{8}}{f_{2}^{5}f_{8}^{4}}. (2.4)

Combining (2.2)–(2.4) yields

∑n=0∞c⁡(n)​qn\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c(n)q^{n} =2​q​f2​f4f12​∑n=0∞(−1)n​aB​(n)​qn+q3​ω​(−q4)+f12​f482​f25​f84−f⁡(q8)2.\displaystyle=2q\frac{f_{2}f_{4}}{f_{1}^{2}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}a_{B}(n)q^{n}+q^{3}\omega(-q^{4})+\frac{f_{1}^{2}f_{4}^{8}}{2f_{2}^{5}f_{8}^{4}}-\frac{f(q^{8})}{2}. (2.5)

and

f12=f2​f85f42​f162−2​q​f2​f162f8.\displaystyle f_{1}^{2}=\frac{f_{2}f_{8}^{5}}{f_{4}^{2}f_{16}^{2}}-2q\frac{f_{2}f_{16}^{2}}{f_{8}}. (2.7)

Substituting (2.6) and (2.7) into (2.5), we obtain

∑n=0∞c⁡(n)​qn\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c(n)q^{n} =2​q​f2​f4​(f85f25​f162+2​q​f42​f162f25​f8)​(∑n=0∞aB​(2​n)​q2​n−∑n=0∞aB​(2​n+1)​q2​n+1)\displaystyle=2qf_{2}f_{4}\left(\frac{f_{8}^{5}}{f_{2}^{5}f_{16}^{2}}+2q\frac{f_{4}^{2}f_{16}^{2}}{f_{2}^{5}f_{8}}\right)\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{B}(2n)q^{2n}-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{B}(2n+1)q^{2n+1}\right)
+q3​ω​(−q4)−f⁡(q8)2+f482​f25​f84​(f2​f85f42​f162−2​q​f2​f162f8).\displaystyle\qquad+q^{3}\omega(-q^{4})-\frac{f(q^{8})}{2}+\frac{f_{4}^{8}}{2f_{2}^{5}f_{8}^{4}}\left(\frac{f_{2}f_{8}^{5}}{f_{4}^{2}f_{16}^{2}}-2q\frac{f_{2}f_{16}^{2}}{f_{8}}\right). (2.8)

(2.9)

≡2​f22​f45f82+q​ω​(−q2)−f28​f82f14​f45(mod8).\displaystyle\equiv 2\frac{f_{2}^{2}f_{4}^{5}}{f_{8}^{2}}+q\omega(-q^{2})-\frac{f_{2}^{8}f_{8}^{2}}{f_{1}^{4}f_{4}^{5}}\pmod{8}. (2.12)

Here we have used the fact that for all positive integers mm and kk,

It follows from [6, Entry 25, (v) and (vi), p.40] that

(2.15)

It follows from (2.2) that

For n≥0n\geq 0,

c⁡(32​n+23)\displaystyle c(32n+23) ≡0(mod8),\displaystyle\equiv 0\pmod{8}, (2.22)

Now, we turn to prove Conjecture 1.5.

Replacing nn by 8​n+38n+3 in (2.1) and employing (2.21), we see that for n,k≥0n,k\geq 0,

c⁡(22​k+5​n+11⋅4k+1+13)≡0(mod4).\displaystyle c\left(2^{2k+5}n+\frac{11\cdot 4^{k+1}+1}{3}\right)\equiv 0\pmod{4}.

The above congrence implies that (1.5) is true when k≥1k\geq 1. Congruence (1.1) implies (1.5) holds when k=0k=0. Therefore, Congruence (1.5) is true for k≥0k\geq 0.

Replacing nn by 8​n+58n+5 in (2.1) and employing (2.22), we see that for n,k≥0n,k\geq 0,

c⁡(22​k+5​n+17⋅4k+1+13)≡0(mod8),\displaystyle c\left(2^{2k+5}n+\frac{17\cdot 4^{k+1}+1}{3}\right)\equiv 0\pmod{8},

from which with (1.2), we arrive at (1.6).

Replacing nn by 16​n+1216n+12 in (2.1) and employing (2.23), we see that for n,k≥0n,k\geq 0,

c⁡(22​k+6​n+38⋅4k+1+13)≡0(mod4).\displaystyle c\left(2^{2k+6}n+\frac{38\cdot 4^{k+1}+1}{3}\right)\equiv 0\pmod{4}.

Congrence (1.7) follows from the above congruence and (1.3). This completes the proof of Conjecture 1.5.  

3 Conclusions

As seen in Introduction, integer partitions in which each part may occur in two colors have received a lot of attention in recent years. In this note, we prove a conjecture posed by Banerjee, Bringmann and Bachraoui [4] on infinite families of congruences for the coefficients of C⁡(q)C(q). Banerjee-Bringmann-Bachraoui’s conjecture implies two conjectures due to Andrews and Bachraoui [2]. A natural problem is to extend the congruences in this paper to modulo 1616, 3232, etc. In addition, it would be interesting to determine the arithmetic density of the set of integers such that c⁡(n)≡0(mod2k)c(n)\equiv 0\pmod{2^{k}} for some fixed positive integers kk.
